w: Session 5 has two halves, both by Dr. Litz. Furcation Management is his recorded lecture, which the Oct 15 quiz covered. Resective Osseous Surgery he taught in person on Oct 15, after the quiz, from his slides; that class also went back over the furcation points he most wants you to know. Furcation vs. furcation defect A furcation is a normal anatomical region of a multi-rooted tooth (premolars and molars) where the roots diverge from the root trunk, a finding as normal as a cusp tip. A furcation defect is what periodontal infection makes of it: destruction of the soft tissue and bone between the roots, seen as clinical attachment loss into the furcation. The point Dr. Litz called arguably the most important of the lecture, and repeated throughout: attachment loss that involves the furcation dramatically decreases the prognosis of the tooth. Furcations are extremely hard to instrument and even harder for the patient to clean, so check for them at every exam: the initial exam, routine prophy checks and periodontal maintenance. Terms and the root trunk The root trunk runs from the CEJ to the first point where the roots diverge (the furcation entrance). The individual roots beyond it are also called root cones. The root complex is the root trunk plus the length of the root cones, CEJ to apex. The furcation fornix is the roof of the furcation (the floor of the root trunk), and divergence is the distance, in millimeters, between the roots. The root trunk carries about 30% of a molar's attachment and the individual roots the other 70%, though trunks vary from person to person and tooth to tooth. Short root trunks are much more likely to get furcation involvement: with a 2 mm trunk, 2 mm of attachment loss already reaches the furcation. A long root trunk is initially favorable, since it takes far more attachment loss to reach the furcation, but once the furcation is involved it complicates therapy: these teeth are generally poor candidates for root resection and other treatments, and because a root's total length is finite, a long trunk means short roots, so little support is left by then. Where the entrances are Dr. Litz called these very important numbers to know (Bower, 1979), measured from the CEJ. Maxillary first molar: three entrances, the mesiopalatal about 3.6 mm, the buccal about 4.2 mm and the distopalatal about 4.8 mm. Another slide rounds these to about 3.5, 4 and 5 mm. Mandibular first molar: two entrances, buccal about 2.4 mm and lingual about 2.5 mm, significantly shorter than the maxillary ones, so a probing depth of 4-5 mm on a molar may already mean the furcation is exposed. (The class exam-review guide lists maxillary entrances of 3, 3.5 and 5 mm; the order is the same.) On maxillary molars the straight buccal entrance is generally narrower than the mesiopalatal and distopalatal ones, whose roots splay farther apart. As a general rule the first molar has a shorter root trunk than the second molar. On mandibular molars, the lingual angulation of the tooth puts the lingual furcation a little more apical than the buccal (a slide also lists the lingual entrance as more than 4 mm from the CEJ and more than 0.75 mm wide). The mesial root is wider buccolingually than the distal, with an hourglass or kidney-bean cross-section and furrows and concavities on its furcal surface. Maxillary premolars: about 40% have two roots, with a mean furcation entrance about 8 mm from the CEJ, a long root trunk with short roots. The maxillary first premolar has a mesial developmental depression (about 0.5 mm) next to the furcation, present 100% of the time, which floss misses even when the patient flosses well. Why furcations are so hard to clean 81% of furcation entrances are less than 1 mm wide, and 58% are less than 0.75 mm wide, while the face of a curette blade is 0.75-1.10 mm wide. So even with profound anesthesia, plenty of time and a new sharp Gracey, most of the time the blade is wider than the entrance; even narrow ultrasonic tips struggle. His extracted maxillary molar showed it: the convex palatal root surface was glass-smooth, while inside the furcation were calculus and granulation tissue left by repeated SRP. Convex surfaces are easy to clean (the root presents the calculus to you); concave surfaces are much harder, especially in a hard-to-reach place. Root depressions facing the furcation: on the maxillary first molar, the mesiobuccal root has a 0.3 mm depression 94% of the time, the distobuccal root 0.1 mm (31%) and the palatal root 0.1 mm (17%). On the mandibular first molar it gets worse: the mesial root has a 0.7 mm depression 100% of the time and the distal root 0.5 mm (99%). In closed SRP you can't see these, and the patient has almost no chance of cleaning them daily, even with a proxy brush. Prevalence Multi-rooted teeth with short root trunks get furcation involvement after minimal attachment loss and often have a less favorable prognosis than single-rooted teeth or teeth with long trunks. Maxillary molars are affected more often than mandibular molars. On maxillary molars the buccal furcation is the most commonly affected, followed by the mesiopalatal and then the distopalatal. On mandibular molars, the buccal furcation is affected most. Contributing factors The primary cause of furcation involvement is progressive clinical attachment loss from inflammatory periodontal disease, that is, plaque. He expects that question on every periodontal exam in dental school and on boards. Other factors contribute: Root trunk length, a key factor in both whether a furcation becomes involved and which treatments are possible. Root form: curvature and fluting raise the risk of root perforation during endodontic therapy, which can lead to furcation problems. Interradicular dimension: closely approximated or fused roots keep instruments out, in SRP and in surgery; widely spaced roots are better for both. Cervical enamel projections (CEPs): see below. Enamel pearls: balls of enamel, most common in the furcations of molars. Connective tissue can't attach to enamel and the pearl's shape holds plaque. On a radiograph, a radiopaque semicircle in the furcation suggests one. Small ones may be removed, usually with surgical access and a finishing bur. Iatrogenic factors: restoration overhangs near a furcation hold plaque and raise inflammation, bone loss and CAL. Restorative margins apical to the free gingival margin should stay within the confines of the sulcus. Intermediate bifurcation ridge: a convex ridge of cementum running mesiodistally across the furcation entrance of a mandibular molar, connecting the mesial and distal roots. It leaves a domed area above it that, once exposed, traps plaque where neither you, the hygienist nor the patient can reach. Cervical enamel projections Dr. Litz singled these out as a definite test question, and more important than that, something to know for life. A CEP is an apical projection of enamel from the CEJ that approaches or enters the furcation: a narrow, wedge-shaped extension (like a widow's peak) pointing from the CEJ toward the furcation. It forms when amelogenesis fails to halt before root formation. Because junctional epithelium and connective tissue can't attach to enamel, the gingiva lies over it without attachment, and the CEP acts like a funnel leading plaque straight into the furcation: a biologic weak link that lowers resistance to furcation involvement. CEPs are more common on mandibular molars (about 30%) than maxillary molars (about 15%), and more likely on second molars and on the buccal than the lingual, mesial or distal. The grades go by how far apically the CEP reaches: Grade 1: a distinct change in the CEJ, pointing apically toward the furcation. Grade 2: the CEP approaches the furcation but does not enter it. Grade 3: the CEP extends into the furcation. Treatment rests on one fact: new attachment will not form on enamel. If there is no bone or attachment loss with the CEP, often the case with Grades 1 and 2, usually no treatment is needed; watch it. If bone or attachment loss is associated with it, remove the CEP. Thin enamel comes off with a diamond or finishing bur (usually through a flap; sometimes without one if it's very shallow). If the enamel is thicker, removal can be attempted with care not to expose the pulp, and on a vital tooth, warn the patient about possible thermal sensitivity. His broader rule: a lone furcation involvement in an otherwise periodontally stable patient should prompt you to look for a CEP. One deep site on one tooth in a healthy mouth means something specific to that tooth (a CEP, an overhang, retained cement, a vertical root fracture on an endodontically treated tooth). Classifying furcations Furcations are examined with the curved Nabers probe, inserted gently under the free gingival margin to feel for the entrance; it takes seconds. The Glickman classification (1953), the one Dr. Litz uses: Grade I: probing into the flute of the furcation, but the interradicular bone is intact (incipient). You can feel the entrance but can't engage it. Grade II: interradicular bone is lost but not through to the opposite side. The probe engages; pulled toward the occlusal, it meets resistance. Grade III: a through-and-through lesion; the probe passes from buccal to lingual. Grade IV: through-and-through with gingival recession, so you can see through it without a probe. The Hamp classification (1975), common among periodontists, grades horizontal loss in millimeters: degree 1, less than 3 mm into the furcation; degree 2, more than 3 mm but not through; degree 3, through-and-through. Both Glickman and Hamp describe horizontal destruction. Tarnow and Fletcher (1984) add a vertical subclass in 3 mm steps: A, 0-3 mm; B, 4-6 mm; C, 7 mm or more. The deeper, the worse the prognosis. Finding them: probing and radiographs The buccal entrance of maxillary molars and the buccal and lingual entrances of mandibular molars are easy to reach with a Nabers probe. The mesiopalatal entrance of a maxillary molar sits offset toward the palatal (the mesiobuccal root is broad), so probe it from the palatal. The distopalatal entrance lies about midway between buccal and palatal, so it can be probed from either side; Dr. Litz stays on the palatal after checking the mesiopalatal. On radiographs, furcation bone loss can come from periodontitis, endodontic infection, root perforation or occlusal trauma. A mandibular molar's two roots make furcation bone loss easy to see. On maxillary molars it's harder because of superimposition: bone loss in the buccal furcation is often masked by the palatal root. Mesiopalatal and distopalatal lesions often show a furcation arrow, a small triangular radiolucency pointing into the furcation. About 30-55% of Grade II or III involvements show one. A furcation arrow on the film means furcation involvement is highly likely, but many involved furcations show none, so it must never be the sole diagnostic tool. His rule for all of dentistry: do the clinical exam first, reach a diagnosis, then use the radiographs to confirm it. Probing (perio probe and Nabers probe) gives the presence and extent of involvement, the attachment level relative to the furcation, and the extent and shape of the defect; radiographs give the interdental bone level and the bone within the root complex, and root shape. Take both periapicals and vertical bitewings. In one study (Ross and Thompson, 1980), clinical exam alone detected furcation involvement in only 3% of maxillary and 9% of mandibular molars; adding radiographs raised it to 65% of maxillary but only 23% of mandibular molars. Use both. Deciding to treat The mere presence of furcation involvement is not by itself an indication for treatment. Active inflammatory periodontal disease and its local factors decide. Removing plaque and calculus (and contaminated cementum) is always the most important step, but a local factor also has to be removed itself: a CEP, an overhang or residual calculus left in place means more attachment loss six months later. Early furcation involvement usually needs no therapy unless there is a local factor that can be altered. Moderate to advanced furcations have a significant horizontal component; the goal is a local environment the patient and hygienist can keep free of further attachment loss, and the most successful long-term approach is to minimize or eliminate the furcation. The two treatment objectives: 1. eliminate microbial plaque from the exposed surfaces of the root complex, and 2. establish an anatomy that lets the patient control plaque. Non-surgical options: SRP (Phase I), chemotherapy (locally delivered antibiotics after SRP, covered in a later lecture) and odontoplasty or furcation plasty. Surgical options: open flap debridement, the tunnel approach, the additive approach (regeneration), resective surgery, and extraction with implant placement. Recommendations by class: Class I, SRP, removal of local factors and furcation plasty. Class II, furcation plasty, regeneration (GTR), root resection or extraction. Class III, tunnel preparation, root resection or extraction. Whether a furcated tooth is worth treating also depends on the degree of involvement (Class I and shallow Class II do better than deep Class II and Class III), the remaining support around the whole tooth, probing depths, mobility, endodontic involvement, tooth position and occlusion, the tooth's strategic value (a non-functioning #31 with no #2 opposing it may not be worth saving), the patient's health and their oral hygiene. Nothing works if the patient can't keep the area clean. Surgical options The most basic is a periodontal flap with debridement: sulcular incisions and a full-thickness flap give access and visibility. If the bone loss is horizontal, without a vertical component, thorough debridement often resolves the inflammation and reduces probing depth. Adding odontoplasty (reshaping tooth: removing a CEP, reducing an intermediate bifurcation ridge) or osteoplasty (reshaping bone to reduce the volume of the defect) makes the furcation shallower and easier for the patient to clean. Regeneration asks whether lost bone in the furcation can be regrown, and it needs careful selection. Poor patients for it: uncontrolled diabetes, immunocompromise, smokers, poor compliance or hygiene. The best teeth are mandibular and buccal maxillary degree II furcations. Interproximal maxillary degree II furcations are significantly less suited because of limited access. For degree III furcations, regenerative therapy gives no better outcome than conventional surgery. In favor: a thicker biotype, no soft-tissue recession, and interproximal bone sitting coronally. Root proximity may impair regeneration; a root canal filling is not a contraindication. The procedure: sulcular incisions and a full-thickness flap; clean the exposed root (by hand instruments, ultrasonics or rotary instruments; without this nothing regenerates); remove enamel projections or pearls; fill the furcation with bone graft and/or cover it with a GTR membrane secured by a resorbable sling suture; secure the flap coronally; then no mechanical plaque removal at the site for up to 4 weeks, using chlorhexidine instead. Success is judged on a radiograph about a year later, as bone fill. Tunneling deliberately removes bone from the furcation to make a tunnel through it, surgically creating a Glickman Grade IV, so the patient can pass an interproximal brush through. It's for deep Class II and Class III defects and is limited to mandibular molars with sufficiently long, divergent roots. Its problem: caries in tunneled molars is common, since root surfaces decay quickly. It's rarely done now that implants exist. Root resection (root amputation) removes one or more roots at the level of the furcation while the crown and remaining roots stay in function. The most common root removed is the distobuccal root of the maxillary first molar. It's limited to deep Class II and Class III defects, aims to eliminate the furcation as a maintenance problem, and commits the patient to endodontic and restorative treatment. It's still used, for example when the bridge abutment #31, already root-canal treated, fractures its mesial root while the distal root is sound: the fractured root is removed and the bridge is kept. Hemisection removes a root and the associated part of the crown, usually on mandibular molars, turning a multi-rooted tooth into a single-rooted one. Implants have made it much less common: it means an endodontist, then the periodontist, then the restorative dentist, over many expensive visits. The sequence for root separation or resection: endodontic treatment first, with the access filled directly with amalgam or composite; a provisional restoration; then root separation and resection, avoiding exposing the interradicular bone, leaving parts of the furcation fornix behind, perforating the canals, or leaving sharp angles on the remaining roots; periodontal surgery to remove bone defects around the remaining roots, with provisional margins ending at least 3 mm coronal to the bone crest; and the final restoration, with a rigid framework for the weakened abutments and an occlusion that minimizes lateral forces. In class: the furcation points he repeated Before the new material, Dr. Litz went back over the recorded lecture. A furcation is normal anatomy; the problem is a furcation defect, and once a furcation is involved the prognosis of the tooth dramatically falls, because we can barely clean it and the patient almost never can. He asked again for the entrance numbers ("I want you to know these numbers"): maxillary first molar mesiopalatal 3.6, buccal 4.2, distopalatal 4.8 mm; mandibular buccal 2.4 and lingual 2.5 mm. So when a molar probes 4, 5 or 6 mm, assume one or more furcations are already exposed. Most entrances are narrower than a curette blade, and every root surface facing into the furcation is concave, which hides calculus where a convex root hands it to you. Asked why maxillary molars break down, he pointed to their less dense bone and their thin facial bone, since these molars tend to sit pushed toward the facial. A thin cervical enamel projection usually comes off with a finishing bur, such as a 7404, in light feather strokes; warn the patient about thermal sensitivity if it's thick. One isolated deep site in an otherwise healthy mouth means something is going on with that one tooth: a CEP, an overhang, residual cement, or a vertically fractured root on a root-canal-treated molar, which means the tooth comes out. He finds furcations with a Nabers probe on every multi-rooted tooth and prefers the Glickman classes, which the school uses too. Phase I, re-evaluation and when surgery comes in In general dentistry, Phase I removes active disease (extract hopeless teeth, endodontics, periodontal therapy) and Phase II is restorative. In periodontics, Phase I is oral hygiene instruction (always first), scaling and root planing, control of plaque-retentive features (overhanging margins, open contacts, odontoplasty for things like CEPs, often only reachable once a flap is raised) and the Phase I re-evaluation. Phase II is surgery, followed by periodontal maintenance (supportive periodontal therapy, recall). Phase I aims to reduce or eliminate gingival inflammation, eliminate pockets produced by edematous enlargement of inflamed gingiva, create an environment that the patient can keep clean, which he called the therapeutic goal for almost every patient (we clean their teeth two to four times a year; they clean them 700 to 800), and improve the surgical manageability of the tissue: firm, with minimal bleeding. That is why a patient can't skip Phase I and go straight to surgery, even one you know will need it: a surgeon clears an infected laceration before setting the fracture under it, and inflamed gingiva bleeds heavily and shreds when a flap is raised. The re-evaluation comes about 4 to 6 weeks after Phase I, when root planing has had its maximum effect, the flora is most favorable and hygiene is at its best. It asks: Is initial therapy complete (etiologic factors controlled, adequate hygiene, no plaque or calculus, inflammation controlled, reduced probing depths)? Is the periodontal status maintainable (shallow or deep pockets, remaining attachment, esthetics, challenges during maintenance)? Can the patient benefit from Phase II surgery: resective surgery, regeneration, open flap debridement or soft-tissue grafting? Three paths follow. Shallow pockets and good hygiene: periodontal maintenance every 3 to 4 months. Plaque everywhere, bleeding and pockets: back through Phase I, reviewing hygiene and debriding again. Good hygiene but deep pockets that a brush and floss can't reach: a surgical candidate. The treatment goals: control plaque to a level compatible with health, eliminate contributing risk factors (furcations, CEPs, overhangs), arrest the disease and prevent recurrence. His slides list 11 indications for periodontal surgery, led by access for root debridement and pocket elimination by removing soft or hard tissue; the others are removing diseased tissue to favor new attachment, correcting mucogingival defects, contours that make hygiene easier, esthetics, a favorable restorative environment, drainage of acute problems, exploratory procedures to determine the prognosis, biopsy, and regeneration. Access matters because root planing has limits. A 1981 study he still cites found a high correlation between residual calculus and pocket depth: in 3 to 5 mm pockets the chance of failure becomes greater, and over 5 mm failure dominates, for three reasons: more surface area to clean, more irregularities as the pocket deepens (furcations at 3.6, 4.2 and 4.8 mm), and an apical part that narrows until the bottom can't be reached. A flap lets you see the root, like doing a filling with your eyes open. Osseous surgery: why remove bone The primary objective of osseous surgery is to eliminate periodontal pockets and create a shallow gingival sulcus the patient can keep clean, with a bony architecture that matches a physiologic gingival architecture. Gingiva is scalloped, like a child's drawing of ocean waves, higher interproximally and lower on the midfacial, and it returns to that shape after surgery even if the bone underneath does not. His most important slide: if the bone does not follow the overlying gingival architecture, the pockets will recur. Ochsenbein defined resective surgery as a procedure to eliminate bony deformities so that bone and gingiva are consistent with each other and the pocket is reduced or eliminated. Treating bone loss by removing bone sounds backwards, he said, but sometimes you fight fire with fire. Periodontitis leaves an uneven bone crest and deep pockets, especially where bone is lost vertically between teeth. In health, the interproximal crest sits about 1 to 2 mm from the adjacent CEJs on a radiograph. Normal alveolar bone has three features: the interproximal bone is more coronal than the labial or lingual bone and pyramidal; the shape of the interdental bone follows the tooth form and embrasure width; and the bony margin mimics the contour of the CEJ. In positive architecture the interproximal crest is coronal to its midfacial and midlingual height, the healthy pattern and the goal. In negative (reverse) architecture it is apical, a crater with deep pockets between the teeth. Flat architecture lies between. When reaching positive architecture would mean removing too much facial and lingual bone, as around a deep interproximal defect between #28 and #29, he settles for flat rather than weaken the tooth. The cost is small. Properly performed osseous surgery removes on average about 0.6 mm of supporting bone height around the tooth. Bone is taken from the facial and lingual or palatal, and interproximal bone is preserved, because the facial and lingual surfaces are smaller, so removing bone there costs less support. Teeth are more mobile after osseous resection, but mobility returns to pre-operative levels after about a year (Selipsky, 1976); warn the patient beforehand. Indications and contraindications Resective surgery is indicated to gain access to an underlying structure (a CEP, a furcation), to remove subgingival bacteria and calculus more effectively, and to reduce or eliminate persistent diseased sites, including bony defects that don't follow the gingival architecture. In practice: active periodontitis that Phase I failed to eradicate; moderate to severe pockets with limited improvement after root planing (the slides say over 4 mm and in furcations; in class he put the line at about 5 mm); mild to moderate horizontal bone loss; 2-wall crater defects and shallow 1-, 2- and 3-wall defects; better access to shallow furcation defects; removing ledges and exostoses such as buccal exostoses and lingual tori, where the gingiva meets the tooth at almost a right angle and can't be cleaned; and creating positive architecture. The goal at the root is a knife-edge approximation of bone to tooth and convex rather than concave contours. The contraindications: ineffective plaque control, the big one ("there's not a periodontist on this earth that doesn't know this"), which the re-evaluation is there to catch, since surgery cures nothing and only creates an environment the patient can keep clean; noncompliance with the treatment plan, such as wanting to skip Phase I; shallow pockets, where surgery or root planing causes attachment loss; a hard-tissue defect amenable to regeneration, which should be regenerated instead (Session 6); an anticipated unacceptable cosmetic result, such as long maxillary anterior teeth in a patient with a high smile line; and uncontrolled systemic disease. Ostectomy, osteoplasty and the steps Ostectomy removes tooth-supporting bone, the alveolar bone proper that is part of the attachment apparatus, to reach a more physiologic form. Osteoplasty reshapes the alveolar process without removing supporting bone: bone with no attachment to the tooth, so it can be thinned more aggressively, even on the facial, as long as it doesn't touch the root (Friedman, 1955). The steps: 1. vertical grooving interproximally (osteoplasty, with large round burs such as a #6 or #8), 2. radicular blending, 3. flattening the interproximal bone, and 4. gradualizing the marginal bone, the conservative ostectomy on the facial and lingual that brings back positive architecture. The most important step of all is thorough debridement of the root surfaces: "if these are not clean root surfaces, nothing is going to work," whether you reshape bone or graft it. Around maxillary molars, treat the mesiobuccal and distobuccal roots as if they were separate teeth: remove bone on the facial of each root, but never take down the bone in the furcation. Exposing it lowers the prognosis, and that bone is hard to get back. Flaps are closed with silk sutures, removed after a week. Patients should know what to expect: longer teeth, exposed roots with possible thermal sensitivity (topical agents help), and open embrasures that trap some food but can now be cleaned with interproximal brushes. His resident case was a three-unit bridge from #3 to #5 that the patient couldn't clean under; bridges are among the most breakdown-prone areas in any mouth. After Phase I, surgery corrected the flat and negative architecture while preserving the furcation bone, and six months later the gingiva was healthy and an interproximal brush fit under the pontic: the whole point of the procedure. And if the patient doesn't clean, none of it works.
